questions.q: Per the lesson, what does a reviewer typically look at first in a governance portfolio?
options: The job candidate's college transcript
A random SQL script, chosen at will
The one-page summary or executive presentation
The RACI matrix's formatting and font choice
questions.explain: The lesson states reviewers typically start with the one-page executive summary — the 'can you explain it in one page' test.

questions.q: What is the signature follow-up question the lesson pairs with a RACI matrix?
options: "How many colors are used in this diagram?"
"What font was used to create this document?"
"Who typed this document?"
"Who is the single Accountable role here, and why that person and not someone else?"
questions.explain: The lesson lists this exact question as the one a RACI matrix needs to survive, tied to the single-A rule from earlier in the path.

questions.q: What should the glossary excerpt in a portfolio demonstrate, according to the lesson?
options: The total number of tables in the source database
A list of every employee's email address
That every term in the database has been renamed
Specific definitions with named owners, not just a restatement of table and column names
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against a glossary that's just a thin restatement of the schema, and asks for specific, owned definitions.

questions.q: Which item appears on the lesson's pre-share checklist?
options: Every artifact must be anonymous, with no named author
Every document is clearly marked as a fictional training capstone (LTV Global)
All documents must be printed, never shared digitally
Numbers are allowed to differ between documents as long as they're close
questions.explain: The checklist explicitly requires every document to be marked as the fictional training capstone, and requires numbers to match across documents, not just be close.

questions.q: What habit from Data Quality Management, Lesson 18 does the lesson say SQL checks in a portfolio should demonstrate?
options: Avoiding JOINs entirely
Only ever running SELECT * with no filtering
Writing the WHERE clause for the failure condition, not the success condition
Never using a WHERE clause in any query
questions.explain: The lesson ties the SQL review step directly back to writing checks that select for the failure condition, the habit built in Data Quality Management, Lesson 18.
